scenes.tts: Mice that lack T R P M eight, the cold and menthol receptor, were trained for ten days to report warming of the forepaw. They completely failed. That sounds backwards. A cold receptor should matter for cold. So why would a mouse without it miss warmth?

scenes.visual: Ten training-day squares fill; a chain warming, TRPM8-null mouse, report ends in a red cross; a TRPM8 chip points to cold with a solid arrow and to warmth with a dashed arrow and a large question mark.
scenes.narration: Mice that lack TRPM8, the cold and menthol receptor, were trained for ten days to report warming of the forepaw. They completely failed. That sounds backwards. A cold receptor should matter for cold. So why would a mouse without it miss warmth?

scenes.tts: Here is the task. A head-fixed mouse is trained to report a temperature step on its forepaw. A Peltier surface, eight by eight millimetres, holds thirty-two degrees Celsius, then steps. Trained mice reported a warming step of one degree. The mouse licks to report it.
scenes.caption: Here is the task. A head-fixed mouse is trained to report a temperature step on its forepaw. A Peltier surface, 8 by 8 mm, holds 32 °C, then steps. Trained mice reported a warming step of 1 °C. The mouse licks to report it.
scenes.visual: A forepaw blob rests on a labelled Peltier plate; a temperature plot holds a 32 degree baseline then steps up by 1 degree, the plate turns yellow, and a lick chip appears.
scenes.narration: Here is the task. A head-fixed mouse is trained to report a temperature step on its forepaw. A Peltier surface, 8 by 8 mm, holds 32 °C, then steps. Trained mice reported a warming step of 1 °C. The mouse licks to report it.

scenes.tts: Alongside the behaviour, the group recorded single fibres from forepaw skin, kept alive outside the animal with its nerve attached. This is a skin-nerve preparation. Each tick is one spike. They warmed the skin at one degree per second. One population, the polymodal C fibres, increased its firing as the skin warmed. Warming excites them.

scenes.visual: A skin bar with one fibre ending labelled polymodal C fibre; a temperature ramp is drawn beneath and the spike ticks of the fibre speed up as the ramp rises.

scenes.tts: A second population answered the opposite way. These are cool-sensitive C fibres, about nineteen percent of the thermosensitive fibres recorded. In a bath at twenty-seven degrees, they fired all the time, between zero point two and six hertz. Warming reduced that ongoing rate. The group used twenty-seven degrees because thermal imaging showed awake forepaw skin at twenty-six to twenty-eight. At the usual thirty-two degree bath, this population had not been seen.
scenes.caption: A second population answered the opposite way. These are cool-sensitive C fibres, about 19% of the thermosensitive fibres recorded. At the usual 32 °C bath, this population had not been seen.
scenes.visual: The same layout with a cool-sensitive fibre: ticks fire steadily before the ramp, then thin out as the ramp rises; the 27 degree bath, the rate range, the imaged skin temperature and the usual 32 degree bath are written in.

scenes.tts: Temperature is not read off one channel at a time. Warmth has two signals at once. Some fibres speed up. Cool fibres slow down. Without T R P M eight, the cool fibres lose their ongoing firing, and one part of the warmth signal is gone. Write that as reduced cool input. Here, no central circuit that flips the sign of the cool signal has been identified.

scenes.tts: Remember the bath. A signal that looks absent at one baseline may be there at another. The resting condition is part of the stimulus, not a neutral background. In the mouse forepaw, warmth is read from excitation and from silence.

scenes.visual: Both rows again; a bracket marks the resting firing of the cool row and is labelled part of the stimulus; chips excitation plus silence combine into warmth.
